stages.geology: Remote sensing, geochemistry, historical maps and outcrops provide the first observations of a region, forming the geological foundation for later engineering.
stages.seismic: Use seismic waves to investigate the subsurface. Large data volumes and demanding computation make this a major area for deep-learning applications.
stages.drilling: Turn a planned trajectory into a borehole. Real-time prediction and optimization must operate within strict safety constraints.
stages.mudlogging: Collect first-hand lithology and fluid evidence behind the bit. Dense but noisy samples and expensive labels favor small-sample recognition methods.
stages.welllog: Continuous downhole measurements offer well-defined tasks, accessible data and labelable examples for early AI applications.
stages.cementing: Long-term isolation depends on a successful cement job. Acoustic logs and operational data support evaluation and design, with high costs for misinterpretation.
stages.completion: Choose how the well connects to the reservoir. Experience and analogous wells make this a useful setting for knowledge-based recommendations.
stages.perforation: Create the final flow path into the reservoir. Surrogate models and knowledge bases can shorten design cycles when field feedback is slow.
stages.production: Rich operating data and measurable feedback support applications such as dynamometer diagnosis and production forecasting.
stages.workover: Infrequent, expensive interventions depend heavily on experience. Case libraries, knowledge graphs and information extraction support planning.
stages.eor: Modify the reservoir or fluid to improve recovery. Long, costly trials make surrogate models especially useful for screening designs.
stages.transport: Pipelines and stations have many sensors but few abnormal events. Reliable detection must carefully control false alarms.
stages.refining: Established process models and extensive DCS measurements support soft sensing and optimization alongside physical models.

cv: Analyze images, volumes and plotted curves: cuttings, borehole images, seismic sections, remote imagery and dynamometer cards.
ts: Forecast, segment and detect anomalies in well logs, drilling parameters, production histories and pipeline pressure.
nlp: Extract, generate and retrieve information from mud-logging reports, workover cases, laboratory records and design documents.
opt: Use parameter search, surrogate models, clustering and inversion for fracturing, injection allocation, formulation screening and recommendations.
kg: Connect entities and past cases to support completion selection, fishing-tool matching and operational recommendations.

g1: Multispectral, hyperspectral and SAR observations reveal surface lithology, structures and alteration for geological mapping.
Segment lithologies and lineaments pixel by pixel, producing vector candidates for review.
Manual interpretation is slow and subjective; vegetation and weathering obscure boundaries.
Geological labels are scarce and transfer between climates or rock assemblages is difficult.
Multispectral or hyperspectral scenes with at least 20 refined lithology masks; historical vector maps as weak labels; matching DEM elevation and slope.
g2: Soil hydrocarbon and related indicators provide indirect evidence of microseepage across hundreds or thousands of sites.
Combine multivariate anomaly detection and spatial clustering to identify candidate targets.
Pollution, terrain and seasonality affect thresholds; the distinction between background and anomalies is subjective.
Strong spatial correlation requires spatially blocked validation to avoid inflated performance.
300–3000 sites per area; 5–10 chemical indicators; 3–5 known targets for validation; geological and remote-sensing background layers.
g3: Scanned historical maps contain legends, faults, annotations and borehole columns that must be digitized for spatial analysis.
Combine symbol detection, OCR and legend rules to extract vector elements.
Manual digitization is labor-intensive, and legend conventions differ across historical periods.
Broken-line topology and inconsistent legends remain difficult even with established detection and OCR methods.
Scans above 300 dpi; at least 200 symbols per class; a legend-to-meaning table; at least 2000 checked lines of annotation text.
g4: Outcrop fracture density, orientation and aperture help characterize fractured reservoirs.
Segment and skeletonize fracture traces in photos and drone imagery; use calibration to estimate orientation and density.
Manual compass and tape measurements are slow, inaccessible in some locations and subject to sampling bias.
Thin low-contrast fractures are hard to detect; geometric calibration is necessary for physical measurements.
200–500 calibrated photos per outcrop; at least 1000 labeled traces; centimeter-resolution drone point clouds; 100–200 field measurements for validation.
s1: Interpreters trace fault surfaces across many sections of a 3D seismic volume to guide structural modeling and well placement.
Predict fault-likelihood volumes with 3D networks and extract surfaces for expert quality control.
Manual interpretation takes weeks; small deep faults are easily missed and interpretations can disagree.
Fault labels are sparse and highly imbalanced; frequency and noise differences complicate cross-survey transfer.
3D SEG-Y amplitude volumes, derived coherence or curvature volumes, and historical fault interpretations; labeled sections across 5–10 surveys.
s2: Seismic facies summarize reflection patterns associated with depositional environments and guide reservoir prediction.
Classify slices or small seismic cubes using well-calibrated facies labels.
Subjective facies boundaries and sparse well control make regional extrapolation uncertain.
Sparse well labels favor weak or semi-supervised learning; facies definitions themselves may be subjective.
10,000–100,000 slices or cubes per area; 50–200 well-calibrated labels; log interpretations, core descriptions and depositional analogs.
s3: First-arrival times influence static corrections and subsequent seismic imaging.
Predict arrival times from shot-gather waveforms using sequence models.
Millions of traces make manual picking costly; low-signal traces produce large errors and rework.
Inference cost, surface waves and strong interference challenge reliability on noisy traces.
100,000–1,000,000 shot traces per survey; labels on 5–10% of traces; source and receiver coordinates; targeted labels on low-signal examples.
s4: Inversion turns seismic observations into estimates of porosity, sand thickness and other reservoir properties.
Learn a nonlinear seismic-to-property mapping using joint well and seismic constraints.
Conventional workflows are lengthy and non-unique, especially with limited well control.
Sparse wells and mismatched well–seismic scales can produce visually plausible but physically unreliable results.
Amplitude, frequency and impedance volumes; interpreted properties from 20–50 wells; facies and sandbody models as constraints.
s5: Surface waves, multiples and industrial noise obscure reflections and require extensive processing.
Use supervised or self-supervised networks to suppress noise while retaining signal.
Numerous processing parameters require experience; aggressive denoising can remove weak reflections.
Clean field targets are rarely available, creating a synthetic-to-field domain gap.
10,000–100,000 noisy traces; forward-modeled clean/noisy pairs; interpreter-labeled noise zones with at least 500 traces per type.
d1: Lithology, weight on bit, rotation, flow and drilling fluid interact to determine drilling speed.
Learn operating-parameter responses and recommend settings within torque, pressure and stability constraints.
Adjustment lags formation changes, while conservative settings limit drilling efficiency.
Extrapolation affects downhole safety; rigs and formations have different operating distributions.
Drilling parameters sampled every 1–10 seconds; lithology and formation intervals; event labels for sticking, losses and gas influx.
d2: Sticking, losses and influx can be preceded by subtle torque, pressure and return-flow changes.
Model normal multivariate behavior and issue graded, interpretable anomaly warnings.
Weak precursors overlap normal fluctuations, while fixed alarms produce misses and false positives.
Incident examples are rare and highly imbalanced; false alarms are costly.
More than ten drilling channels; incident times, types and responses; operational-state labels derived from parameter rules.
d3: Directional drilling adjusts toolface and sliding intervals to keep the borehole within target windows.
Combine model-predictive control with learned formation responses to suggest steering settings.
Experience-dependent corrections can cause trajectory fluctuations, friction and inefficient sliding.
Downhole response identification and safety validation make advisory deployment more practical than full autonomy.
Survey stations every 10–30 m; toolface and sliding records by stand; formation dip and lithology as disturbances.
d4: Alternating loads accumulate fatigue damage that can lead to costly drillstring failures.
Extract damage features from vibration and torque histories to estimate remaining life.
Footage or drilling-time rules do not capture damage differences between operating conditions.
Rare failures call for hybrid modeling that combines fatigue physics with time-series evidence.
High-frequency vibration and torque; tool type and service histories; inspection, wear and failure records.
d5: Fluid density, viscosity and filtration affect wellbore stability and cuttings transport.
Predict property changes from circulation and return measurements and suggest treatment quantities.
Infrequent manual tests delay detection; experience-based dosing can overshoot and oscillate.
Sparse laboratory labels must be aligned with high-frequency circulation measurements.
Fluid tests once or twice per shift; continuous flow, temperature and pressure; treatment type, dose and time.
m1: Mud loggers inspect cuttings to describe composition, grain size and hydrocarbon shows.
Use fine-grained image classification and multilabel recognition to estimate lithological composition.
Frequent, small and mixed samples create subjective descriptions and uncertain labels.
Similar lithologies, imbalance, mixing and contamination complicate recognition.
300–800 microscope images per well with scale and controlled light; at least 500 examples per lithology; descriptions and sample-handling records.
m2: Total hydrocarbons and gas composition provide rapid evidence of hydrocarbon shows while drilling.
Detect anomalous gas intervals and suggest fluid types using sequence models.
Mud properties, extraction efficiency and connection gas distort peaks and obscure thin intervals.
Anomalies are scarce and testing for ground truth is expensive.
Gas measurements every 1–5 m; 200–500 labeled anomalous intervals; drilling-fluid parameters; formation tests and production verification.
m3: UV fluorescence intensity and color help assess oil shows and fluid character in cuttings.
Extract color and intensity features to suggest oil-show grades with visual evidence.
Visual grades vary with operators, UV sources and imaging conditions.
Consistent lighting, distance and exposure are essential for transfer between wells.
200–600 controlled UV images per well; graded cuttings descriptions; limited formation-test verification.
m4: Time spent drilling each meter indirectly reflects drillability and changes in lithology.
Segment drilling-time curves and cross-check boundaries against cuttings and gas logs.
Operating parameters and sample lag can shift or obscure apparent formation boundaries.
Single-curve evidence is limited; inaccurate lag correction can systematically corrupt labels.
Drilling-time curves at 0.5–1 m spacing; boundaries from 30–50 wells; weight, speed and flow measurements; matching cuttings and gas logs.
m5: Final logging reports combine stratigraphy, fluid shows, operating events and recommendations.
Extract traceable information from structured records and earlier reports to draft a standard report.
Manual assembly takes hours and creates inconsistencies across tables, authors and conclusions.
Domain terminology, templates and traceability are essential to accurate drafts.
Structured logging records; 100–300 historical reports with annotated information-to-paragraph links; company reporting standards.
w1: Continuous petrophysical curves are divided into geological units used in reservoir interpretation and interval design.
Detect change points with sliding features and optimal segmentation, then review candidate boundaries.
Manual correlation is slow and thin interbeds lead to inconsistent picks.
Data are accessible, but label granularity varies and thin layers are easily missed.
GR, SP, RT and DEN sampled at 0.125 m; boundary tables from 30–50 wells; at least 20 neighboring wells and a shared stratigraphic standard.
w2: Porosity, permeability and saturation are traditionally estimated by core-calibrated log relationships.
Learn nonlinear multi-log mappings constrained by core and formation-test evidence.
Limited cores and complex pore systems make regional empirical formulas unreliable.
Depth matching errors and cross-area transfer require careful calibration with local examples.
Conventional and special logs; 50–200 core-analysis samples per well; formation tests and production validation.
w3: Electrical and acoustic images show wall textures, fractures, vugs and bedding.
Segment fractures and vugs to support density, orientation and aperture interpretation.
Manual tracing is slow; low-angle and induced fractures can be confused.
Thin shapes and similar appearances demand costly expert labels.
Full-depth borehole images; 500–2000 fracture masks; core fracture descriptions; interpreted density and orientation tables.
w4: Multi-log crossplots help assign lithologies, often using manually selected regional boundaries.
Fuse several curves to classify lithology and express class uncertainty.
Fixed boundaries struggle with complex volcanic, carbonate and mixed lithologies.
Class imbalance and varying responses within one lithology remain major obstacles.
Conventional and spectral gamma logs; 100–300 core or cutting labels per well; thin-section identification for label quality.
w5: Missing intervals, abrupt artifacts and washouts can distort downstream interpretation.
Reconstruct missing signals using masked or cross-curve models and report uncertainty.
Manual interpolation lacks evidence and may violate consistency between curves.
Missing values have no direct truth; downstream interpretation provides only indirect evaluation.
Multiple logs with marked anomalous intervals; neighboring-well references; caliper and engineering records.
c1: CBL and VDL measurements support interval-wise assessment of cement bonding and zonal isolation.
Classify acoustic and variable-density responses into candidate bonding grades.
Manual evaluation is slow, and fast formations or microannuli can lead to consequential mistakes.
Subjective grading and special conditions require dedicated examples and careful validation.
Full-depth CBL/VDL logs; 100–300 graded intervals; slurry and job records; pressure tests or remedial-work verification.
c2: Slurry density, rheology, rate and displacement design must achieve isolation without losses.
Model displacement efficiency and recommend a slurry program within the density window.
Neighbor-well designs can fail in narrow pressure windows, leaving losses or channels.
Limited jobs and multifactor outcomes create noisy training targets.
Caliper, temperature and pressure windows; density, rate and return-height records from hundreds of jobs; CBL and loss outcomes.
c3: Cement losses can reduce cement height or require repeat work, making pre-job assessment valuable.
Estimate loss risk from well conditions and slurry design and identify influential factors.
Small errors in pressure or equivalent density can change risk assessments in narrow-window wells.
Loss events are imbalanced and interpreted pressure inputs carry their own uncertainty.
200–1000 jobs with pore/fracture pressures and caliper; slurry-column designs; loss occurrence and volume.
c4: Casing centralization controls cement-ring uniformity and the risk of narrow-side channels.
Calculate stand-off and optimize centralizer positions and spacing.
Empirical spacing may underperform in irregular boreholes and is difficult to verify before running casing.
Geometry provides the main model; optimization supports an interpretable placement design.
Caliper and deviation surveys; casing and centralizer dimensions and placement; cement-bond feedback.
co1: Open-hole, perforated, screened and gravel-pack completions serve different reservoir and sanding conditions.
Link reservoir attributes, completion choices and outcomes in a knowledge graph to rank analogous designs.
Experience-based choices become difficult in new areas without comparable wells.
Productivity, sand control and cost compete; models can rank alternatives rather than define one universal optimum.
100–500 wells with reservoir and fluid attributes; completion types and production outcomes; design reports for knowledge extraction.
co2: Shot density, phasing and penetration balance productivity against rock strength and sanding risk.
Use surrogate models and multiobjective search to propose Pareto-efficient designs.
Standard designs overlook combinations that depend on well geometry and local conditions.
Physical simulation is needed to supplement limited field samples.
Rock mechanics and reservoir parameters; designs and test production from 200–500 wells; sanding and intervention records.
co3: Temperature and pressure changes generate tubing loads and deformation that can cause buckling or leakage.
Use surrogates to screen loads and safety factors across many operating conditions.
Evaluating combinations is slow, encouraging overly conservative designs.
Mechanistic simulation can supply training data; rare field failures are useful for validation.
String geometry, steel grades and depths; simulated temperature/pressure/production scenarios; failure and leakage records.
co4: Segmented sleeves can balance inflow and limit water, but control sequences interact across intervals.
Learn sleeve-control policies in a reservoir simulator to improve cumulative production.
Fixed openings or fully open sleeves overlook inter-segment interactions.
Reliable simulation is essential; field validation is costly and slow.
Segment properties and water saturation; interval production, opening and pressure histories; a reservoir simulation environment.
p1: Shot density, phasing, penetration and charge type control the final well-to-reservoir flow path.
Combine surrogate prediction and multiobjective search for reservoir-specific designs.
Standard parameters may be reused across dissimilar reservoirs without quantifying the loss.
This overlaps completion design and benefits from shared modeling with distinct scenario views.
Stress, strength and permeability; historical designs and test rates from 200–500 wells; sanding and intervention constraints.
p2: Tunnel penetration and cleanliness determine effective flow area and depend on rocks, stress and charge performance.
Train a surrogate on numerical simulations to rapidly compare tunnel shapes.
Target tests are expensive and individual simulations are too slow for broad screening.
Simulation-to-field differences require calibration against limited target tests.
Charge and target properties; measured penetration and diameter; tunnel CT images or casts where available.
p3: Charge selection trades penetration, hole diameter and casing damage against reservoir and completion conditions.
Structure charge specifications and applicability rules in a knowledge graph to rank candidates.
Manual references become outdated and familiar charges may not suit a specific well.
The core task is structured retrieval and rule matching using manufacturer information.
Manufacturer charge specifications; lithology and casing grade/thickness; field performance feedback.
p4: Well tests and production provide indirect evidence of perforation efficiency and skin.
Infer efficiency, identify weak intervals and support decisions about additional perforation.
Most wells have limited test data, leaving weak quantitative evidence for interval-level decisions.
The inverse problem is non-unique and needs geological constraints.
1000–10,000 production, pressure and water-cut records per well; perforation intervals and settings; limited test-derived skin estimates.
pr1: Load–displacement dynamometer cards reveal states such as insufficient inflow, gas lock, pump leakage and rod failure.
Classify card images and prioritize abnormal wells for review.
Large well populations prevent daily manual inspection; complex and combined conditions are less consistent.
Well-defined classes and abundant data help, but difficult cases still need expert review.
1–24 cards per well per day; 50,000–100,000 labeled cards; stroke, speed, pump size and liquid rates; verified pump-inspection outcomes.
pr2: Well and field forecasts support allocation, intervention selection and development planning.
Use covariate-aware time-series models and examine production changes around interventions.
Simple decline assumptions miss interventions and injection response; short new-well histories are unstable.
Interventions create distribution shifts that purely historical forecasts may not capture.
1000–10,000 daily records per well; workover and stimulation events; injection and neighboring-well covariates.
pr3: Injection allocation balances layer contributions, pressure support and water-cut control.
Optimize layer injection rates using an injection–production response model.
Quarterly manual revisions create long feedback cycles and experience-driven trial adjustments.
Reliable response models are essential, especially in areas with few samples.
Quarterly layer allocations and intake profiles; daily production and water cut; inter-layer connectivity constraints.
pr4: Gas lock, scale, overheating and electrical faults can stop electric-submersible-pump production.
Detect anomalies and degradation in electrical and operating signals to support maintenance planning.
Indirect monitoring and slowly developing failures limit early manual detection.
Fault types are imbalanced and may need different models.
Minute-scale current, voltage, frequency and wellhead pressure; fault and pump-inspection records; water cut, gas–oil ratio and temperature.
pr5: Wax and scale restrict wellbores and flowlines, requiring cleaning or preventive treatment.
Predict deposition risk from production, pressure and temperature and suggest treatment timing.
Fixed cleaning schedules over-treat some wells and miss fast-depositing wells.
Early signals are weak and intervention-derived labels have uncertain timing.
Daily operating data; cleaning method, date and effect; wax content and wax-appearance temperature.
wo1: Fault-specific procedures and tool combinations affect workover duration and success.
Connect symptoms, procedures, tools and outcomes to retrieve analogous cases and rank plans.
Planning depends on experience and inconsistent historical records.
The quality of entity and relationship extraction controls recommendation quality.
500–2000 well interventions; well histories and fault descriptions; designs, summaries and operation durations.
wo2: Lost tubing, rods, tools and cables require tools matched to their dimensions, shape, depth and well geometry.
Classify fish attributes and match tool–procedure combinations using a knowledge graph.
Trial tool runs and manual handbook searches increase trips and time.
Small datasets and predominantly textual descriptions require careful structuring.
300–1000 labeled fish descriptions or images; fishing combinations and outcomes; casing dimensions and deviation constraints.
wo3: Deformation, corrosion and perforation threaten integrity and are evaluated with caliper or ultrasonic images.
Detect and grade damage by interval, location and type.
Dense measurements make manual review slow; mild deformation can resemble ordinary ovality.
Rare, varied damage requires graded assessments rather than a simple binary label.
Full-depth multi-finger caliper or ultrasonic data; 500–2000 labeled damage intervals; field verification and well histories.
wo4: Pressure and torque anomalies during fishing, milling and killing may precede secondary incidents.
Perform real-time anomaly detection with graded warnings.
Manual monitoring leaves only minutes between detecting an anomaly and responding.
Very few incidents favor unsupervised baselines over overfitted supervised models.
Second-scale pressure and torque; incident times and types; operational labels for milling, fishing and circulation.
wo5: Operation durations affect lost production, crew schedules and materials planning.
Predict stage durations as intervals using historical interventions.
Similar jobs can vary greatly across wells, undermining experience-based scheduling.
Records use inconsistent daily or shift-level granularity and need harmonization.
Over 1000 jobs per area; operation start/end times; depth and fault features; crew and equipment records.
e1: Stage and cluster design, rate, proppant and fluids influence stimulated volume and productivity.
Train surrogates using fracturing simulations and search parameter combinations.
Neighbor-well recipes often overlook stress and natural-fracture differences.
Surrogate reliability is limited by the underlying simulator’s fidelity.
Stress, brittleness and fracture properties; rate, pressure and proppant histories from thousands of stages; post-treatment production and EUR.
e2: Fracture length, height and conductivity are inferred indirectly from microseismic and treatment measurements.
Fuse microseismic events, treatment histories and geological models to estimate fracture geometry.
Microseismic interpretation is subjective, and treatment inversion admits multiple solutions.
Fracture geometry is rarely observed directly, making the inversion strongly ill-posed.
Thousands of microseismic events; stage pressure, rate and proppant data; tracer and production-profile validation.
e3: Polymer and surfactant recipes require extensive laboratory screening before field trials.
Predict recovery performance from formulations and guide the next experiments.
Weeks-long tests explore only a small part of a large formulation space.
Small datasets and differing test conditions favor active-learning strategies.
Hundreds to thousands of formulation/performance tests; viscosity, temperature and salinity conditions; limited incremental-production field results.
e4: Steam volume, soak duration and withdrawal rates affect cycle production and oil–steam ratio.
Forecast cycle responses and optimize cumulative performance across cycles.
Cycles interact, so a locally good setting may not optimize cumulative recovery.
Individual wells have few cycles; pooling across wells is needed.
10–30 cycles per well; steam volume and quality, soak and liquid production; reservoir/fluid properties and temperature monitoring.
e5: Microbial metabolites influence oil mobility; activity depends on nutrients, temperature and salinity.
Estimate activity and production response from injection and produced-fluid indicators.
Culture tests are slow, and changing communities complicate nutrient replenishment decisions.
Very small samples and uncertain mechanisms limit reliable modeling.
Weekly cell counts, metabolites and pH; daily nutrient injection, production and water cut; limited field incremental-oil measurements.
t1: Pressure waves, flow balance and acoustic measurements support pipeline leak detection and location.
Combine multichannel anomaly detection with hydraulic models to locate candidate leaks.
Small leaks can lack clear pressure waves, while valve and pump operations cause false alarms.
Rare leaks and similar operational disturbances make false-alarm control essential.
Second-scale pressure, flow and temperature across stations; leak locations/times/volumes; valve and pump operation logs.
t2: In-line inspections identify large numbers of corrosion defects for growth and maintenance assessment.
Match defects across inspections and estimate remaining strength and life.
Manual matching is slow and measurement uncertainty distorts growth estimates.
Inspection and alignment errors compound uncertainty in inferred growth rates.
Defect locations, depths and sizes from repeated inspections; matched positions; excavated depth measurements for validation.
t3: Pump and compressor settings influence energy use as production and seasonal conditions change.
Optimize equipment combinations and operating settings using a hydraulic network model.
Conservative operating rules and interactions between stations hinder global optimization.
A reliable network model and explicit safety constraints are necessary.
Network topology, pipe diameters and pump curves; minute-scale flow, pressure and energy; time-of-use prices and production plans.
t4: Instrument drift and scaling introduce systematic errors into multiphase and orifice metering.
Compare instruments and physical models to identify drift and recommend correction or maintenance.
Long calibration intervals allow errors to accumulate between manual inspections.
Well-defined mechanisms and structured data make this a relatively accessible application.
Minute-scale meter readings, temperature and pressure; calibration values and dates; cleaning and maintenance events.
t5: Radar level measurements and video surveillance support tank-farm operations.
Read visual level marks and roof condition, cross-check radar and flag inconsistencies.
Instrument failure lacks independent checks; night and adverse weather limit manual video inspection.
Image quality at night and in fog is a key constraint.
Fixed-camera day/night video; continuous radar level data; alarm and response records.
r1: Cut points, reflux and furnace temperature determine product distribution, quality and energy demand.
Predict product distributions with surrogate models and optimize operating setpoints.
Crude changes require retuning; yield, energy and quality objectives compete.
Models must work with advanced process control and account for complex mechanisms.
Second-scale DCS temperatures, pressures and flows; batch crude density, sulfur and distillation data; laboratory product quality.
r2: Feedstock, reaction temperature and catalyst-to-oil ratio jointly determine catalytic-cracking product yields.
Predict product distributions from feed and operating variables for optimization and scheduling.
Mechanistic calibration is difficult and frequent feed changes increase prediction errors.
Strong coupling and nonlinearity require consistent alignment of feed, operation and product data.
Hourly feed and operating properties; laboratory and online yields; regeneration temperature and catalyst activity.
r3: Unexpected downtime of pumps, exchangers and compressors creates major losses.
Model degradation using vibration and process conditions to estimate remaining useful time.
Fixed alarms miss early degradation and do not transfer between equipment or conditions.
Rare failures but continuous degradation support unsupervised and transfer-learning approaches.
Continuous high-frequency vibration and temperature; maintenance and replacement labels; equipment type and service age.
r4: Large LIMS datasets influence process control and product release decisions.
Combine rules, anomaly detection and language processing to flag questionable results and trace causes.
Manual sampling misses errors and can incorrectly reject valid results.
Explicit, interpretable rules should remain central, with AI supplementing anomaly recognition.
Multivariate, multi-batch LIMS results; reviewer decisions; process-specific normal ranges and rules.
r5: Laboratory octane, flash-point and pour-point results arrive hours after the process conditions they describe.
Estimate quality from process variables in real time and report uncertainty intervals.
Delayed tests reveal quality failures after the fact; online analyzers can be costly to maintain.
Sparse laboratory labels call for mechanistic constraints and semi-supervised learning.
Second-scale temperature, flow and pressure; quality tests once or twice per shift; installed online analyzers as references.
